record.description: Sorabji presents the Cicero and Gellius reports as distinguishing external conditions and internal causes of assent. External impressions are necessary conditions, not sufficient causes; character is internal. Sorabji distinguishes three competing readings of what this establishes and does not locate necessitation exclusively in auxiliary causes.
record.label: Chrysippus's Causal Taxonomy (Causes Perfect/Auxiliary)

conclusion.text: The taxonomy distinguishes external from internal causal contribution; its success in reconciling necessity and responsibility remains disputed.

premises.text: There exists a distinction between perfect and principal causes (causae perfectae et principales) and auxiliary/proximate causes (causae adiuvantes et proximae) in Stoic causal analysis.
An external impression (phantasia) is an auxiliary/proximate cause of assent, not a perfect/principal cause.
The agent's own character or nature (analogized to the cylinder's shape) is the perfect/principal cause of assent and subsequent action.
Universal causal determinism (fatum) obtains: every event has a cause, and causes are themselves caused in an unbroken chain.
External impressions are reported as necessary but not sufficient conditions. Whether the total causal nexus necessitates assent depends on the disputed interpretation of Chrysippus.
Moral responsibility (to eph' hēmin) requires that the agent be the principal cause of the action, not merely that the action be uncaused or contingent upon external circumstances.

validity_assessment.rationale: The argument is formally valid if one grants the Stoic causal framework and the identification of moral responsibility with principal causation. However, scholarly acceptance is disputed: critics (beginning with ancient opponents, e.g., Carneades via Cicero) argue that if auxiliary causes necessitate the occasion of assent and principal causes are themselves antecedently determined, the agent's 'own nature' is not ultimately up to the agent. The 'reconciliation' depends on a compatibilist premise (P6) that many scholars and ancient critics reject as question-begging. Bobzien (1998) argues Chrysippus achieves a coherent compatibilism; others (e.g., Salles 2005, Barnes 1983) dispute whether principal/auxiliary causation successfully preserves anything recognizable as moral responsibility against incompatibilist challenge.

premises.text: External impressions (phantasiai) present themselves to the human soul, initiating but not completing the process of assent.

Just as a cylinder cannot begin to move unless pushed, but the push gives it only the beginning of motion and not its rollability (volubilitas), so too the external impression impresses itself upon the mind but does not give assent.
Assent (synkatathesis) is 'in our power' (in potestate nostra) in the sense that its completion depends upon our internal nature, character, and reason.

Moral responsibility (to eph' hēmin) attaches to the internal cause (character/assent) rather than the external cause (impression), just as we attribute the cylinder's rolling to its shape rather than to the push.
The internal cause (character/assent) is itself fated and determined by prior causes, yet this does not eliminate the distinction between proximate cause (internal) and initiating cause (external).

For Stoic causal analysis, the principal cause (aition) of an action is the agent's character and assent, while external impressions function as proximate/auxiliary causes (sunaitia/prokatarktika); this distinction is sufficient for the Stoic account of responsibility.

validity_assessment.rationale: The argument is formally valid as a conditional chain: if responsibility requires only distinction between internal/external causes (P1-P4), and if internal causes are principal causes (P6), then responsibility is preserved (C). However, scholarly acceptance is deeply disputed: Alexander of Aphrodisias and later critics argue that the argument commits a modal fallacy—conflating (a) 'assent is in our power' in the sense of being internally caused, with (b) 'assent is in our power' in the sense of being open to alternative possibilities. The cylinder analogy only establishes (a), leaving the compatibilist conclusion question-begging against incompatibilist critics. See Bobzien 1998, ch. 6, on the distinction between proximate and principal causes in Stoic theory.
validity_assessment.scholarly_consensus: The argument is widely regarded as Chrysippus's central compatibilist move, but whether it successfully answers the 'freedom question' (as opposed to merely the 'causal location' question) remains contested. The attestation of P4-P6 as 'reconstructed' reflects that Chrysippus likely did not distinguish these as separate argumentative steps; the modern scholarly reconstruction (especially Bobzien 1998; also Salles 2005) separates the causal analysis from the normative conclusion that critics like Alexander challenged.

premises.text: Epicurus held that all events in the physical world are determined by the motion of atoms through the void according to fixed laws of collision and rebound.

Epicurus introduced the atomic swerve (parenklisis / clinamen) as a physical mechanism to account for certain phenomena, including the collision of atoms that initiates compound bodies and voluntary human action.
The atomic swerve was intended by Epicurus to break the causal nexus of atomic determinism at a fundamental level, thereby preserving a non-determined origin for human action.

Prior to Epicurus, no ancient thinker formulated a recognizably incompatibilist position that (a) accepted causal determinism as a genuine threat to human agency and (b) sought a physical or metaphysical solution to preserve undetermined choice.

Aristotle's discussion of voluntariness (to hekousion) in Nicomachean Ethics III.1-5 and Eudemian Ethics II.6-11 concerns exculpation and praise/blame conditions, not the metaphysical compatibility of determinism and free agency; the 'free will problem' in the modern incompatibilist sense is absent from his corpus.

The Stoics, beginning with Zeno and Chrysippus, developed a compatibilist theory of fate (heimarmenē) and assent (sunkatathesis) that explicitly rejected the need for indeterminacy in human action, thereby responding to a problem they did not themselves originate.

record.description: Sint igitur astrologorum percepta huius modi: 'Si quis (verbi causa) oriente Canicula natus est, is in mari non morietur.' Vigila, Chrysippe, ne tuam causam, in qua tibi cum Diodoro, valente dialectico, magna luctatio est, deseras. Si enim est verum, quod ita conectitur: 'Si quis oriente Canicula natus est, in mari non morietur', illud quoque verum est: 'Si Fabius oriente Canicula natus est, Fabius in mari non morietur.' Pugnant igitur haec inter se, Fabium oriente Canicula natum esse, et Fabium in mari moriturum; et quoniam certum in Fabio ponitur, natum esse eum Canicula oriente, haec quoque pugnant, et esse Fabium, et in mari esse moriturum. Ergo haec quoque coniunctio est ex repugnantibus: 'Et est Fabius, et in mari Fabius morietur', quod, ut propositum est, ne fieri quidem potest. Ergo illud: 'Morietur in mari Fabius' ex eo genere est, quod fieri non potest. Omne ergo, quod falsum dicitur in futuro, id fieri non potest.

record.description: Quod si ita est, omnia, quae fiunt, causis fiunt antegressis; id si ita est, fato omnia fiunt; efficitur igitur fato fieri, quaecumque fiant.' Hic primum si mihi libeat adsentiri Epicuro et negare omnem enuntiationem aut veram esse aut falsam, eam plagam potius accipiam quam fato omnia fieri conprobem; illa enim sententia habet aliquid disputationis, haec vero non est tolerabilis. Itaque contendit omnis nervos Chrysippus, ut persuadeat omne axioma aut verum esse aut falsum. Ut enim Epicurus veretur, ne, si hoc concesserit, concedendum sit fato fieri, quaecumque fiant, (si enim alterum utrum ex aeternitate verum sit, esse id etiam certum et, si certum, etiam necessarium; ita et necessitatem et fatum confirmari putat), sic Chrysippus metuit, ne, si non obtinuerit omne, quod enuntietur, aut verum esse aut falsum, non teneat omnia fato fieri et ex causis aeternis rerum futurarum.

De ipsa atomo dici potest, cum per inane moveatur gravitate et pondere, sine causa moveri, quia nulla causa accedat extrinsecus.

record.description: Rursus autem, ne omnes a physicis inrideamur si dicamus quicquam fieri sine causa, distinguendum est et ita dicendum, ipsius individui hanc esse naturam, ut pondere et gravitate moveatur, eamque ipsam esse causam, cur ita feratur. record.description: Quodsi concedatur nihil posse evenire nisi causa antecedente, quid proficiatur, si ea causa non ex aeternis causis apta dicatur? Causa autem ea est, quae id efficit, cuius est causa, ut vulnus mortis, cruditas morbi, ignis ardoris. Itaque non sic causa intellegi debet, ut, quod cuique antecedat, id ei causa sit, sed quod cuique efficienter antecedat, nec, quod in campum descenderim, id fuisse causae, cur pila luderem, nec Hecubam causam interitus fuisse Troianis, quod Alexandrum genuerit, nec Tyndareum Agamemnoni, quod Clytaemnestram. Hoc enim modo viator quoque bene vestitus causa grassatori fuisse dicetur, cur ab eo spoliaretur.

record.description: Chrysippus autem cum et necessitatem inprobaret et nihil vellet sine praepositis causis evenire, causarum genera distinguit, ut et necessitatem effugiat et retineat fatum. 'Causarum enim', inquit, 'aliae sunt perfectae et principales, aliae adiuvantes et proximae. Quam ob rem, cum dicimus omnia fato fieri causis antecedentibus, non hoc intellegi volumus: causis perfectis et principalibus, sed causis adiuvantibus et proximis'. Itaque illi rationi, quam paulo ante conclusi, sic occurrit: si omnia fato fiant, sequi illud quidem, ut omnia causis fiant antepositis, verum non principalibus causis et perfectis, sed adiuvantibus et proximis. Quae si ipsae non sunt in nostra potestate, non sequitur, ut ne adpetitus quidem sit in nostra potestate. At hoc sequeretur, si omnia perfectis et principalibus causis fieri diceremus, ut, cum eae causae non essent in nostra potestate, ne ille quidem esset in nostra potestate.

record.description: Quam ob rem, qui ita fatum introducunt, ut necessitatem adiungant, in eos valebit illa conclusio; qui autem causas antecedentis non dicent perfectas neque principalis, in eos nihil valebit. Quod enim dicantur adsensiones fieri causis antepositis, id quale sit, facile a se explicari putat. Nam quamquam adsensio non possit fieri nisi commota viso, tamen, cum id visum proximam causam habeat, non principalem, hanc habet rationem, ut Chrysippus vult, quam dudum diximus, non ut illa quidem fieri possit nulla vi extrinsecus excitata (necesse est enim adsensionem viso commoveri), sed revertitur ad cylindrum et ad turbinem suum, quae moveri incipere nisi pulsa non possunt. Id autem cum accidit, suapte natura, quod superest, et cylindrum volvi et versari turbinem putat.

Nec vero quisquam magis confirmasse mihi videtur non modo fatum, verum etiam necessitatem et vim omnium rerum sustulisseque motus animi voluntarios, quam hic, qui aliter obsistere fato fatetur se non potuisse, nisi ad has commenticias declinationes confugisset. Nam, ut essent atomi, quas quidem esse mihi probari nullo modo potest, tamen declinationes istae numquam explicarentur. Nam si atomis, ut gravitate ferantur, tributum est necessitate naturae, quod omne pondus nulla re inpediente moveatur et feratur necesse est, illud quoque necesse est, declinare, quibusdam atomis vel, si volunt, omnibus naturaliter . . . .

record.description: Εἶναι δὲ καὶ εὐπαθείας φασὶ τρεῖς, χαράν, εὐλάβειαν, βούλησιν. καὶ τὴν μὲν χαρὰν ἐναντίαν [φασὶν] εἶναι τῇ ἡδονῇ, οὖσαν εὔλογον ἔπαρσιν· τὴν δ’ εὐλάβειαν τῷ φόβῳ, οὖσαν εὔλογον ἔκκλισιν. φοβηθήσεσθαι μὲν γὰρ τὸν σοφὸν οὐδαμῶς, εὐλαβηθήσεσθαι δέ. τῇ δ’ ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐναντίαν φασὶν εἶναι τὴν βούλησιν, οὖσαν εὔλογον ὄρεξιν. καθάπερ οὖν ὑπὸ τὰ πρῶτα πάθη πίπτει τινά, τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον καὶ ὑπὸ τὰς πρώτας εὐπαθείας· καὶ ὑπὸ μὲν τὴν βούλησιν εὔνοιαν, εὐμένειαν, ἀσπασμόν, ἀγάπησιν· ὑπὸ δὲ τὴν εὐλάβειαν αἰδῶ, ἁγνείαν· ὑπὸ δὲ τὴν χαρὰν τέρψιν, εὐφροσύνην, εὐθυμίαν.

record.description: ζῶναί τ’ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς εἰσι πέντε· πρώτη βόρειος [καὶ] ὑπὲρ τὸν ἀρκτικὸν κύκλον, ἀοίκητος διὰ ψῦχος· δευτέρα εὔκρατος· τρίτη ἀοίκητος ὑπὸ καυμάτων, ἡ διακεκαυμένη καλουμένη· τετάρτη ἡ ἀντεύκρατος· πέμπτη νότιος, ἀοίκητος διὰ ψῦχος. Δοκεῖ δ’ αὐτοῖς τὴν μὲν φύσιν εἶναι πῦρ τεχνικόν, ὁδῷ βαδίζον εἰς γένεσιν, ὅπερ ἐστὶ πνεῦμα πυροειδὲς καὶ τεχνοειδές· τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν αἰσθητικὴν 〈φύσιν〉. ταύτην δ’ εἶναι τὸ συμφυὲς ἡμῖν πνεῦμα· διὸ καὶ σῶμα εἶναι καὶ μετὰ τὸν θάνατον ἐπιμένειν· φθαρτὴν δ’ ὑπάρχειν, τὴν δὲ τῶν ὅλων ἄφθαρτον, ἧς μέρη εἶναι τὰς ἐν τοῖς ζῴοις.

record.description: Ἔτι τῶν λόγων οἱ μὲν ἀληθεῖς εἰσιν, οἱ δὲ ψευδεῖς. ἀληθεῖς μὲν οὖν εἰσι λόγοι οἱ δι’ ἀληθῶν συνάγοντες, οἷον εἰ ἡ ἀρετὴ ὠφελεῖ, ἡ κακία βλάπτει· 〈ἀλλὰ μὴν ὠφελεῖ ἡ ἀρετή· ἡ κακία ἄρα βλάπτει〉. ψευδεῖς δέ εἰσιν οἱ τῶν λημμάτων ἔχοντές τι ψεῦδος ἢ ἀπέραντοι ὄντες, οἷον εἰ ἡμέρα ἐστί, φῶς ἐστιν· ἡμέρα δέ ἐστι· ζῇ ἄρα Δίων. καὶ δυνατοὶ δ’ εἰσὶ λόγοι καὶ ἀδύνατοι καὶ ἀναγκαῖοι καὶ οὐκ ἀναγκαῖοι· εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ ἀναπόδεικτοί τινες, τῷ μὴ χρῄζειν ἀποδείξεως, ἄλλοι μὲν παρ’ ἄλλοις, παρὰ δὲ τῷ Χρυσίππῳ πέντε, δι’ ὧν πᾶς λόγος πλέκεται· οἵτινες λαμβάνονται ἐπὶ τῶν περαντικῶν καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν συλλογισμῶν καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν τροπικῶν.

record.description: Reference anthology for Hellenistic philosophy (A.A. Long & D.N. Sedley, 2 vols., Cambridge University Press 1987). Volume 1 = texts translated into English with philosophical commentaries organised by theme; volume 2 = original Greek/Latin texts with textual notes and a selective critical apparatus. LS numbering = the scholarly standard for citing Stoic, Epicurean, Academic sceptical, and Pyrrhonian fragments (e.g. LS 55N for Chrysippean causality). Key sections for the KG: 20 ("Free will" — the Epicurean clinamen, p. 102), 55 ("Causation and fate", p. 333), 57 ("Impulse and appropriateness" — impulse and oikeiôsis, p. 346), 62 ("Moral responsibility", p. 386), 65 ("The passions", p. 410), 68–70 (the Academics, including Carneades, p. 438-467), 71–72 (the Pyrrhonian revival, p. 468-488). Partial French edition: Brunschwig & Pellegrin, Les philosophes hellénistiques (GF Flammarion 2001, 3 vols.).
